Let \(c=f(0)\), and interpret \(f(0)\) on the right side as the constant function equal to \(c\). We will show that

\[
\|T^n(f)-c\|_\infty \to 0.
\]

For \(x>0\),

\[
T(f)(x)=\frac1x\int_0^x f(t)\,dt
      =\int_0^1 f(xu)\,du.
\]

Thus, by induction,

\[
T^n(f)(x)=\int_{[0,1]^n} f(xu_1u_2\cdots u_n)\,du_1\cdots du_n.
\]

Let \(M=\|f\|_\infty\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that

\[
|f(y)-c|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\qquad\text{whenever }0\le y\le \delta.
\]

This is possible by continuity of \(f\) at \(0\).

For any \(x\in[0,1]\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
|T^n(f)(x)-c|
&\le \int_{x u_1\cdots u_n<\delta} \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\,du
   + \int_{x u_1\cdots u_n\ge \delta} 2M\,du.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(x u_1\cdots u_n\ge \delta\) with \(x\in[0,1]\), then each \(u_i\ge \delta\). Hence the measure of the set where \(x u_1\cdots u_n\ge \delta\) is at most \((1-\delta)^n\). Therefore,

\[
|T^n(f)(x)-c|
\le \frac{\varepsilon}{2}+2M(1-\delta)^n.
\]

Taking the supremum over \(x\in[0,1]\),

\[
\|T^n(f)-c\|_\infty
\le \frac{\varepsilon}{2}+2M(1-\delta)^n.
\]

Since \(0<1-\delta<1\), the second term tends to \(0\). Thus for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
\|T^n(f)-c\|_\infty<\varepsilon.
\]

Because \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary,

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\|T^n(f)-f(0)\|_\infty=0.
\]

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
